units.text: Extracting urban patterns in undulating landscapes from SAR data with thresholding approach
Introduction

The extraction of urban footprints from SAR (Synthetic Aperture Radar) datasets in undulating terrains using a thresholding approach is a pivotal area of remote sensing research (Lin et al. 2019;Song and Civco 2004).

into account these complexities, contributing to improved identification accuracy (Gao et al. 2022;Jian et al. 2020;Wang et al. 2021).Moreover, the method's dependence on coherent signal patterns enables differentiation between various urban elements, such as buildings, roads, and green spaces (Engemann et al. 2020;Lobaccaro et al. 2019;Well and Ludwig 2019).This research embraces immense practical significance.Accurate urban footprint extraction in undulating terrains aids urban planning, disaster management, and environmental assessments (Cian et al. 2019;Ile and Ziemelniece 2019).

The urban footprint is used to determine the total extent of a region that comprises urban features such as houses, roads, and other man-made structures (Bixler et al. 2019;El-Deen Taha and Elbeih 2010;Nkwunonwo 2013;Rahman et al. 2020).Remote sensing technology is widely used nowadays for the identification and mapping of various objects on the earth's surface including urban features (Gomarasca 2010;Kumar 2021;Yang et al. 2016).

At present, it has become important to monitor the ongoing rapid urbanization to ensure proper city or town planning.To observe, manage and control the rapid urban sprawl, which is occurring because of urbanization, urban planners require the latest information on an urban area to implement systematic town or city planning strategies and for this data is collected from all available sources.One of the most reliable sources for gathering up-to-date information about an urban area is remote sensing (Carrion et al. 2009;Chen et al. 2021;Hake et al. 2023;Jian et al. 2020;Qabaqaba et al. 2023).This technique is mostly preferred over the traditional mapping method due to its efficiency such as it is less expensive and less time consuming, it gives a continuous spatial coverage with a high level of accuracy and it enables the user to visualize spatial data and create a decision support system model (NISAR 2018;Podest 2018).The use of remote sensing satellite imageries helps in monitoring the land cover changes taking place on the earth's surface.Due to the presence of cloud coverage in optical satellite images is not available for all seasons and hence, the attention has now been moved towards the use of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) technology which has cloud penetrating properties and is independent of any weather condition.Microwave remote sensing technology is widely used nowadays for studies related to urbanization as it has produced good results (Aher and Ph 2014;Brian 2016;Sudhira et al. 2004).Their exclusive properties such as double bounce and corner reflectors also help in determining the landscape of urban features and this method is extensively used for planning, monitoring and various developmental activities (Kumar 2021;Liu et al. 2020).

With the onset of SAR technology, research has been extensively carried out to study the efficiency of using this data for analysing urban objects and excellent results have been attained (Kalm 2007;Mohite et al. 2019; Otay and Yıldız 2021; M. Mahmudur Rahman & Sumantyo, 2010).For assessing the influence of human behaviour on the environment, it is important to analyse the pattern of urban sprawl to observe and estimate the rate of population migration that is taking place because of the population flocking from rural to urban areas in search of jobs and for education purposes (Blaschke et al. 2019;Leiva-Murillo et al. 2013).The SAR image is useful for such applications as it helps in analysing and detecting the pattern of human settlements and for estimating the population of a region (Elshehaby & El-Deen Taha, 2009;Mete et al. 2020;Shareef et al. 2016;Wu et al. 2021).The unique property of SAR image, that is, the double bounce and corner reflectors scattering effects helps in determining the landscape of an urban area as it distinguishes buildings and houses from other objects such as road networks, railways, and open areas (Al Fugara et al. 2009;Blasco et al. 2020;Meerow 2019).The dihedral and the corner reflectors are the main features that represent the buildings from a SAR image (Deepthi et al. 2018;Ratha et al. 2017;Thiele et al. 2006).These dihedral and the corner reflectors are the major contributing factors for understanding and analysing urban objects using SAR imagery (Camps-Valls & Bruzzone, 2009;Maboudi et al. 2018;Rafiee et al. 2019).In addition to this, the SAR image is generated from a high-resolution sensor which makes it an excellent choice for carrying out urban analysis (Aghababaee et al. 2013;Deepthi et al. 2018).

Obtaining urban area information from microwave remote-sensing satellite images through urban footprint extraction is a modern and established technique (Nkwunonwo 2013;Yang et al. 2016).Feature extraction is an image-processing method that extracts various topographical features based on their shape, edge, and texture (Jian et al. 2020;Poormirzaee and Oskouei 2010;Zhang et al. 2010).These features are required to classify the SAR image into various classes such as water bodies, urban areas, vegetation, and others.

This research employs the Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) datasets for studies related to urbanization (i.e., to identify the best threshold values for the extraction of urban features).This analysis is carried out in Kohima Sadar Block using the C-band SAR data obtained from the Sentinel-1 A sensor, and the Google Earth images were also used for validating the extracted urban features.It was found that the best threshold value for identification and extraction of urban areas (i.e., which provided accurate information about the different urban features) was at a Coherence of 0.5.This study aims to address these challenges and enhance the accuracy of urban feature extraction.The proposed technique employs a thresholding approach to capitalize on the coherence properties of SAR data.Coherence acts as indicative of the signal similarity between radar acquisitions and offers insights into changes within urban areas.Selection of an optimal threshold value requires an effective technique to distinguish urban footprints from natural features.

The findings will contribute to optimizing thresholding strategies for SAR-based feature extraction, benefiting both scientific endeavours and real-world applications.As remote sensing technology advances, refining techniques for urban feature extraction becomes increasingly vital, ensuring precise insights into urban dynamics and their intricate interactions with diverse terrains.
Study area and dataset
Study area

Figure 1 Kohima Sadar is an administrative block that falls under Kohima district in the state of Nagaland, India.It is situated at a latitude of 25°41'6.962"N and a longitude of 94°7'28.606"E covering a total land area of 69.84 km 2 .Kohima Sadar is in the central region of the Kohima district and is surrounded by other administrative blocks such as Sechu in the western part, Chiephobozou in the northern part, and Jakhama in the southeastern part.It consists of both rural and urban regions and three villages also come under this block.As per the 2011 Census of India, Kohima Sadar has a household of 26,138 and a total population of 116,870 with the male and female populations being 60,551 and 56,319 respectively.Kohima Sadar is hilly terrain, and the main town area also lies in this block.The assessment carried out based on the 2011 Census showed that 98.2% of the population lives in urban areas and 1.8% of the population lives in rural areas.Kohima Sadar also has a literacy rate of 78.89% with the literacy rate ratio of males and females being 81.21% and 76.39% respectively ( h t t p s : / / w w w .c e n s u s i n d i a 2 0 1 1 .c o m / n a g a l a n d / k o h i m a / k o h i m a -s a d a r -p o p u l a t i o n .h t m l).
Methodology
Properties of sentinel-1 A C-band datasets

Sentinel-1 A C-Band datasets offer valuable radar imagery for Earth observation.It has a wavelength of approximately 3.5 cm and C-Band penetrates clouds and provides day-andnight imaging.The datasets deliver high-resolution images with spatial detail required for monitoring urban, agricultural, and natural areas.The dual-polarization capability of the C-band satellite enhances data interpretation by discerning between different surface types.This offers applications like land cover classification and deformation monitoring.The properties of Sentinel-1 A C-Band datasets allow diverse applications in environmental monitoring, disaster management, and infrastructure planning.The repeat-passes of Sentinel-1 A acquisitions support the interferometry approach for deformation analysis.
a) Ancillary data

The vector layers of the administrative boundary with related attribute tables of the study area are created with the help of GIS tools and toposheets.b) Pre-processing of the Sentinel-1 A SAR Satellite dataset.

Image pre-processing for the Sentinel-1 A SAR dataset has been carried out using the open-source SNAP toolbox.Two SAR imageries of the same month with an acquisition date of 7th January 2020 and 31st January 2020 have been used for the generation of Coherence images.VV co-polarized SAR data is mainly used for the study due to its unique property, which enables vertically oriented ground targets to produce a double bounce to bring a strong return towards the sensor (Correa-Muñoz and Murillo-Feo 2018;Ngo et al. 2021).Multi-looking and terrain correction steps were done for further pre-processing of the Coherence image.Different bands such as Mean dB and Difference dB were also derived using the VV polarization of the Sentinel-1 A SAR dataset which was layer stacked along with the Coherence image which was used as an input for carrying out the urban feature extraction.The urban areas were then extracted by masking out the urban features with threshold values of 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, and 0.7 using the band math tool, and further comparison was done to see which threshold value was best suited for the extraction of urban areas.
Datasets
Satellite images

Sentinel-1 A descending pass satellite data of 7th January 2020 and 31st January 2020 and Sentinel-2 A optical data of 9th November 2020 have been used in this study for performing the urban feature extraction of Kohima Sadar.Image splitting is suggested when the study is confined only to a specific region as it minimizes the processing time.

The meta-data properties of the Sentinel-1 A SAR dataset acquired on 7th January 2020 and 31st January 2020 for the VV polarization can be seen in Table 1.bodies.Coherence plays an important role in distinguishing between urbanized and forested regions (Bruzzone et al. 2004).A low backscattered value has been recorded in the waterbodies of SAR imagery because of specular reflection and this helps in differentiating the various land-cover types.Furthermore, the coherence value of open water is low since the backscattered value obtained for this category is low in both the SAR imageries.High backscattered value has been recorded in the urban regions of SAR imagery which resulted in a high value of coherence.Urban regions have a high value of coherence because of the high backscattered value which was recorded on the SAR imagery.

Urban infrastructures such as metropolises and road networks had a high value of coherence in the two SAR images which were acquired on different days (Abdelkarim et al. 2022;Chettry 2022;Usai 2000).The value of coherence of urban regions is at a threshold of 0.5 to 0.8 (Hang and Anh Tuan 2021).The backscattered value of urban areas in multi-temporal SAR imageries is found to be stable with the coherence being more than 0.5 (Corbane et al. 2018).
Workflow for generation of urban footprint using SAR dataset

Two SAR images of the Sentinel-1 A SLC (Single Look Complex) dataset acquired during different days were used for urban footprint extraction.The SLC data contains both amplitude and phase intensity.Level-1 SLC (Single Look Complex) products are SAR imageries in the slant range by azimuth imaging plane, in the image plane of satellite data acquisition.Each pixel of the image consists of information on both phase and amplitude and is represented by a complex (I and Q) magnitude value (Deepthi et al. 2018).A coherence image is generated using the SLC phase information and the main requirement for generating a coherence image is a pair of Sentinel-1 A SLC SAR images of different dates.The urban areas were masked out using coherence and amplitude.The steps involved in the extraction of urban footprint in the SNAP toolbox using Sentinel-1 SLC data are as follows.

Generation of geometrically terrain-corrected backscattered intensity image using SLC dataset a) Sentinel 1 TOPS Split: Image sub-setting of the two Sentinel-1 data was done to extract out the AOI (area of interest) by selecting the sub-swath and different burst.
b) Apply precise orbit file: In this step, a resituated orbit file is used for updating the abstract metadata of an orbit since the metadata information of SAR products
Characterization SAR coherence data of urban features as per the backscatter responses

Feature identification of urban features using the SAR dataset depends on the backscattered response of the Coherence image.The backscattered signal of a particular feature on the earth's surface is highly dependent on the surface coarseness and the dielectric constant.The signal phase information of the complex SAR images obtained by the InSAR technique helps in determining the interferometric products such as the coherence image and it also allows to measurement of the variation between the two imageries.The accuracy of feature identification with Interferometric SAR imageries is affected by several types of noises like atmospheric pressure, humidity, and temperature (Chini et al. 2019;Jian et al. 2020).Volume scattering and perpendicular baselines also produce additional noises which, in turn, disturb the phase signals of the coherence image (Ferretti et al. 2007).Coherence is measured by evaluating the degree of dependency between the two waveforms.If there is a high correlation between the two waveforms, the coherence is high.However, a low correlation between the two waveforms indicates a low coherence (Woodhouse 2017).The amplitude correlation coefficient of two complex SAR images determines the local coherence which is assessed in a small frame where few pixels are in azimuth and range (Lopez-Martinez et al. 2004) after recompensing the terrain effect.Noise removal can be carried out by performing multi-looking (Ferretti et al. 2007).The value of coherence falls in the range between 0 (presence of just phase noise) to 1 (interferometric phase noise is absent).b) The following conditional algorithms as seen in Table 2 were used for the extraction of urban footprints:

Estimation of SAR coherence

Coherence is the measurement of the amplitude of two complex SAR imageries which comprise two components i.e., magnitude and phase information.The magnitude ranges between 0 and 1, where 0 means no correlation and 1 means perfect correlation (Abdel-Hamid et al. 2021).Figure 3 shows the calculated SAR coherence image in the study area over the urbanized and non-urbanized regions.The coherence value for the study region is in the range of 0.12 to 0.74.High coherence areas are white, corresponding to built-up areas, and have high backscatter.
Urban feature extraction based on threshold approach

After the coherence estimation step, the changes within the study area were distinguished by applying different thresholds to the coherence imagery and the best threshold value for the extraction of urban features was identified.There are presently a lot of methods for automatically selecting thresholds for analysing and extracting urban areas but due to the presence of speckle noise in the coherence image, there is difficulty in choosing a global threshold value (Hang and Anh Tuan 2021).

The values of coherence between 0.4 and 0.7 are verified for urban regions.The study on land cover classification and analysis with coherence imagery shows that the values for extraction of urban objects are from 0.5 to 0.99 (Corbane et al. 2018;Usai 2000).Conditional algorithms were used for the extraction of urban footprints and the description of thresholding conditions for the coherence threshold of 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, and 0.7 can be seen in Table 2.

Interpretation of the urban feature based on RGB of sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 dataset

The urban features extracted using the coherence image at a threshold of 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, and 0.7 were visually interpreted It is observed that at a threshold of 0.5, the distribution of urban features pixel values of the coherence image and RGB imageries of Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 data falls in the same position which makes the value of 0.5 a suitable threshold for the extraction of urban features.At the same time, according to the InSAR theory, if the value of coherence of an object on a pair of SAR interference images is more than 0.5 it is called a correlation.Henceforth, the value of 0.5 was selected as the best threshold for the identification and extraction of urban objects on a coherent image.The SAR image classification for the study of urban areas is done in the VV polarization where the value towards 1 represented urban classes and the value towards 0 represented the non-urban classes.

The selection of the best threshold value was further validated by taking three locations on the high-resolution of the first acquisition represents the green band and the intensity imagery of the second acquisition represents the blue band (Catherine et al. 2006).The urban footprint at a coherence threshold of 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, and 0.7 is overlaid on RGB of Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 data (as shown in Figs. 5 based on the RGB of Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 images, and the best threshold for the estimation of urban areas was identified.The RGB image of Sentinel-1 data is created using the coherence and intensity images where the coherence imagery represents the red band, the intensity imagery Fig. 5 Urban footprint at a coherence threshold of 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, and 0.7 overlaid on RGB of Sentinel 1 data good phase correlation between the two acquired images due to the high scene stability.This evaluation includes a comparison among the selected four threshold values (i.e., 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, and 0.7) to find the best threshold value for and 6 ) which is used as a reference to precisely examine the urban areas in the study region.The extracted urban features are overlaid in red colour and have a high level of backscatter and coherence which represents an extremely location where the presence of urban areas is identified which indicates that the most suitable value for the extraction of urban features for the study area is at a coherence threshold of 0.5.The backscattered sigma nought value of the urban features at a coherence threshold of 0.5 is greater than 0 dB and hence the urban features over the study area are well overlaid.

Figure 5(d), Fig. 5(e), Fig. 6(d), and Fig. 6(e) display the urban footprint extracted from Sentinel-1 at a coherence threshold of 0.6 and 0.7 respectively overlaid on the RGB of Sentinel-2 datasets.The results show that the urban features extracted at a coherence threshold of 0.6 and 0.7 do not yield good results as some of the urban feature pixels are missing though the remaining of the urban feature pixels fall in the position comprising of an urban area.The backscattered sigma nought value of the urban features at a coherence threshold of 0.6 and 0.7 is also found to be greater than 0 dB as it has extracted only the urban features despite missing out some pixels of urban features which is highly dependent on the value of the backscattered coefficient.
Validation of the best threshold for extraction of urban features in selected locations

Google Earth image was used for the validation and identification of the most suitable coherence threshold value at a micro-level for the extraction of urban features at three selected locations in the study area which comprises mainly urbanized zones.The selected three locations can be seen in Fig. 7.

The selection of the best threshold value was further validated by taking three locations on the high-resolution imagery of Google Earth which can be seen in Fig. 7.The extracted urban features at a threshold of 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, and 0.7 were then overlaid on the selected three locations as seen in Figs. 8 and 9,and Fig. 10 for evaluating the best threshold for the estimation of urban regions.

Figure 8 (a-e) displays the Google Earth imagery of Location 1 which covers the High school colony, Lower Bayavu Hill, and the locality towards Billy Graham Road.Urbanization is spreading slowly towards these zones since the main town or municipal area is getting overpopulated and compact.Location 1 has a minimum elevation of 1372 m with a minimum and maximum elevation of 1348 m and 1417 m respectively.It has an elevation gain of 132 m and an elevation loss of -68.4 m.The maximum slope is found to be 52.4% (-57.7%) and the average slope is 15.6% (-12.6%).The information obtained for the elevation profile runs over the urbanized zones from top to bottom of location 1.

The findings show that the urban features extracted at a coherence threshold of 0.4 do not represent the urban regions very well as the urban feature pixels are falling not only in the urban regions but also in the areas having vegetation and forest cover.The extracted urban areas have a high coherence and backscatter coefficient value.The backscattered values present in the extracted urban areas fall in the range where the value of sigma nought is greater than 0 dB but less than − 20 dB.However, the backscattered value of urban features is supposed to be greater than 0 dB or a value nearing 1.This finding explains why the non-urban features were also included while extracting the urban features at a coherence threshold of 0.4 hence this threshold value is not suitable for the extraction of urban features in the study region.

Conclusion

The current study presents an approach for the detection of urban infrastructures from the SAR dataset.Several surface features can be extracted further to provide useful information about any area.The study extracts urban footprints from the coherence images, and it is observed that the built-up objects have a higher coherence value in the range of 0.4 to 0.7.Comparative analysis exhibits that the extracted urban features at a coherence threshold level of 0.5 provide a superior result.The comparative visualisation for validation of the Google Earth images reports that the urban pixels at a coherence threshold of 0.5 match the exact locations.Although this coherence image looks viable for the identification of the urban regions, it is impossible to distinguish the barren areas with road features due to the low coherence and backscatter response value from these features.The information on urban footprint extraction from the SAR datasets for hilly terrains may be very useful in studying the trends of urban sprawl.The current work can be further expanded to carry out a similar study in different polarizations of the SAR dataset to progress a better understanding of the impact of radar geometry and backscattered values for obtaining information on urban areas with a high level of accuracy.

a) The contribution of SAR imagery towards the identification and monitoring of urban features irrespective of any weather condition.b) One of the key findings in the study was that the result obtained at a coherence threshold value of 0.5 is the most suitable for the identification and extraction of urban features in the study area.c) The study area comprises hilly terrain with a mean elevation of 1300 m and a minimum and maximum elevation of 700 m and 1900 m respectively (Kikon et al. 2022).Despite the presence of a flat terrain which is considered to be more suitable for urbanization, a good amount of urbanization is present in the study region even though limited space is available for the construction of buildings and this shows that the rate of urbanization is not reliant on the elevation profile of a region but is dependent on several factors such as social, economic and political issues which combine by circumstances of modernization and this draws the people to migrate from rural to urban areas in search of employment opportunities and for educational purpose and this leads to the building of houses in any open space available or even in landslide-prone zones to accommodate the growing population.d) Radar geometry also plays an important role in the study of urban feature extraction using the SAR dataset.The study region has a maximum slope of 59.3% (-66.7%) and an average slope of 21.9% (-19.8%) with a mean incidence angle of 69.39°.All these factors are also the major determining factors for the study of urban areas using SAR imagery.The incidence angle of a SAR image defines the angle between the ground, the sensor, and the surface normal of the irradiated surface.

The incidence angle strongly influences the backscattered coefficient of a SAR image as it helps in determining the scattering properties and their interactions with the ground surface.A strong backscattered value is expected if the slopes are tilted towards the sensor but in the case where the slopes are tilted away from the sensor, a weak backscattered value is expected.However, the scattering property is highly dependent on the different categories of land surface features.

c) Radiometric Calibration: The pixel values of the SAR imagery are converted to a radiometrically calibrated sigma-nought backscatter intensity image.The GRD datasets consist of the metadata information which contains the calibration parameters of the sensor that helps in computing the backscatter intensity.The image intensity values are converted to sigma naught values which are used to determine the strength of the return echo in a distributed target based on the geometric cross-section.The variation of the sigma nought values depends on the change in the wavelength, incidence angle, type of polarization, and surface properties of scattering values.d) TOPS Deburst: Debursting was done to remove the gaps between the various bursts and to combine the images to form a single image.e) Multi-Looking: Multi-looking is performed to generate square pixels with equal dimensions since the debursted image is in SLC format and the pixel dimensions between x and y are not the same.Multi-looking also reduces the speckles to some extent and enhances the image quality by averaging out the pixels in one dimension.f) Conversion of Linear Bands to Decibels (dB): The linear bands are converted to logarithmic scale (dB) for better visualization of the SAR image.g) Range Doppler Terrain correction/Geometric Correction: The earth's topography causes various geometrical distortions such as shadows and foreshortening which need to be rectified.Terrain correction was done using the SRTM 30-meter Digital Elevation Model (DEM) to correct such distortions.h) Convert to Decibels (dB): The geometrically corrected image is converted to a logarithmic scale (dB).
